• Operability (15%) — how much expertise the platform demands day to day.

Published MITRE ATT&CK Evaluation results informed the correlation and coverage assessments; we did not conduct our own testing.

The Question That Should Decide Your Shortlist

Native XDR or open XDR?

Native XDR — Palo Alto, CrowdStrike, Microsoft, SentinelOne, Trend Micro correlates telemetry the vendor collects itself. Correlation is deeper and faster because the vendor controls the data format end to end. The cost is consolidation: you get the most value by buying that vendor’s endpoint, network, and cloud products too.

Open XDR ingests third-party telemetry as a first-class citizen, letting you keep the tools you have. Correlation is generally shallower because the data is less consistent, but you avoid a rip-and-replace.

The honest guidance: If you are already substantially standardized on one of the big platform vendors, native XDR gives you dramatically better outcomes for less effort.

If your estate is genuinely heterogeneous and will stay that way, an open approach or a modern SIEM with automation and detection engineering is usually the more realistic answer than pretending a native platform will correlate your other vendors’ data well.

The trap to avoid: buying a native XDR platform and then feeding it third-party data via generic connectors. You pay platform prices for SIEM-quality correlation. Decide which model you’re in before you take quotes.

The Platforms, Scored 1. Palo Alto Cortex XDR — 8.8/10 Palo Alto Cortex XDR cross-source incident correlation dashboard

Why it scores here: perfect scores on data coverage and correlation. Cortex XDR was the platform that defined the category, and its native fusion of endpoint, network, cloud, and identity telemetry remains the deepest here.

Strengths: Strengths: Genuine cross-source correlation that meaningfully reduces alert volume; strong behavioural analytics and identity analytics; excellent for organizations running Palo Alto firewalls, where network context arrives natively; validated resilience across Palo Alto Cortex XDR operations.

Trade-offs: delivers most value inside a Palo Alto estate; data ingestion pricing requires careful modelling and is where budgets overrun; deployment and tuning demand more effort than endpoint-only platforms; openness score reflects that third-party sources are supported but second-class.

Ideal buyer: Palo Alto–standardized enterprises with a SOC.

Verify before buying: model your data ingestion volume and cost explicitly.

Image ALT: Palo Alto Cortex XDR cross-source incident correlation dashboard

2. CrowdStrike — 8.5/10 CrowdStrike Falcon XDR incident correlation and threat graph

Why it scores here: near-top across the board, with the strongest detection engineering and the best threat intelligence context of any platform here.

Strengths: Exceptional endpoint telemetry as the foundation; Falcon extends natively into identity, cloud, and log management, functioning alongside the best EDR security tools; OverWatch managed hunting adds human expertise; adversary attribution turns incidents into actionable context; strong API and automation.

Trade-offs: modular pricing accumulates quickly across the XDR surface; log ingestion and retention costs need modelling; the July 2024 content update incident makes update-staging controls a required evaluation topic for this vendor and every other.

Ideal buyer: enterprises wanting best-in-class detection with a managed hunting layer.

Verify before buying: which modules you actually need, and the ingestion cost of the data sources you’ll add.

Image ALT: CrowdStrike Falcon XDR incident correlation and threat graph

3. SentinelOne Singularity — 8.3/10 SentinelOne Singularity XDR data lake and automated response

Why it scores here: the only perfect response automation score, plus the best openness score among the native platforms — Singularity Data Lake ingests third-party telemetry more willingly than most native XDR.

Strengths: Strongest autonomous response and rollback backed by enterprise malware protection solutions; Storyline correlation assembles attack narratives automatically; genuinely usable third-party data ingestion; good operability for teams without deep expertise.

Trade-offs: data coverage breadth trails Palo Alto and Microsoft; automated response requires tuning; the platform has expanded broadly, so scope carefully.

Ideal buyer: organizations with small security teams that need automation to compensate for headcount.

Verify before buying: data lake ingestion pricing at your log volume.

Image ALT: SentinelOne Singularity XDR data lake and automated response

4. Microsoft Defender XDR — 8.2/10 Microsoft Defender XDR unified incident view across identity and endpoint

Why it scores here: excellent coverage and correlation across Microsoft’s own enormous surface — endpoint, identity, email, cloud apps, and Azure — with the lowest openness score here, which is the trade.

Strengths: Correlation across Entra ID, Office 365, Intune, and endpoint is genuinely powerful and hard to replicate; built-in capabilities that automatically isolate compromised devices reduce triage load; included in Microsoft 365 E5, which makes the economics extraordinary if you already hold it; enormous telemetry advantage.

Trade-offs: third-party telemetry generally requires Microsoft Sentinel alongside, which is a separate cost and skillset; licensing complexity across Defender products is the most common source of confusion; the console rewards Microsoft ecosystem familiarity.

Ideal buyer: Microsoft 365 E5 organizations, where this is close to a default.

Verify before buying: whether your third-party data needs push you into Sentinel, and what that costs at your volume.

Image ALT: Microsoft Defender XDR unified incident view across identity and endpoint

5. Trend Micro Vision One — 7.9/10 Trend Micro Vision One XDR workbench and risk insights

Why it scores here: strong coverage — Trend correlates endpoint, email, server, cloud workload, and network natively, and email is a data source several competitors handle less completely.

Strengths: Email as a first-class XDR source matters, since that’s where most attacks begin; excellent server and cloud workload coverage; strong vulnerability research heritage bridging endpoint security EDR vs XDR; good value at platform scale; risk insights that prioritize exposure alongside detection.

Trade-offs: correlation quality trails Palo Alto and CrowdStrike; the platform is broad, making licence scoping genuinely difficult; console complexity reflects the breadth.

Ideal buyer: organizations where email and server workloads are the primary risk surface.

Verify before buying: the credit-based consumption model and what your actual usage implies.

Image ALT: Trend Micro Vision One XDR workbench and risk insights

6. Cisco XDR — 7.4/10 Cisco XDR incident correlation with network and third-party telemetry

Why it scores here: good coverage and the second-best openness score — Cisco built XDR with third-party integration as a stated design goal rather than an afterthought.

Strengths: Genuinely open to third-party telemetry; strong network context from Cisco’s networking estate, Virtual Private Network (VPN) architectures, and Secure Network Analytics; Talos intelligence; good fit for organizations with Cisco networking but mixed security tooling.

Trade-offs: endpoint detection depth trails the specialists; correlation quality is good rather than leading; licensing complexity typical of Cisco.

Ideal buyer: Cisco networking estates with heterogeneous security tools.

Verify before buying: which of your existing tools are supported natively versus by generic connector.

Image ALT: Cisco XDR incident correlation with network and third-party telemetry

7. Trellix — 7.4/10

Why it scores here: solid across coverage and correlation, drawing on the combined McAfee Enterprise and FireEye detection portfolio spanning endpoint, network, email, and sandbox.

Strengths: Broad native detection estate to correlate; strong heritage against targeted attacks; on-premises deployment available where cloud is not permitted; open architecture positioning with a large integration library for enterprise SOC tools.

Trade-offs: portfolio consolidation since the merger warrants a direct roadmap conversation; operability scores lowest here — the platform demands more from administrators; new buyers should compare carefully against the leaders.

Ideal buyer: existing Trellix estates consolidating detection.

Verify before buying: current portfolio naming and product roadmap.

Image ALT: Trellix XDR platform correlation across endpoint, network and email

8. Fortinet — 7.3/10 Fortinet Security Fabric XDR automated cross-product response

Why it scores here: good coverage and automation with high operability, driven by the Security Fabric — if your network, endpoint, email, and cloud are all Fortinet, correlation and automated response come cheaply.

Strengths: excellent value inside a Fortinet estate; automated Fabric-wide response without human involvement; strong network telemetry; manageable by generalist IT teams.

Trade-offs: Lowest openness score alongside Microsoft — value collapses outside the Fabric; endpoint detection depth trails the specialists. Fortinet’s exploited-vulnerability record, including items listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, makes patch discipline essential.

Ideal buyer: Fortinet-standardized organizations.

Verify before buying: how much of your telemetry actually originates in the Fabric.

Image ALT: Fortinet Security Fabric XDR automated cross-product response

9. Sophos — 7.3/10 Sophos XDR guided investigation and cross-product detection

Why it scores here: the only perfect operability score in this list. Sophos XDR is the platform a two-person IT team can genuinely run, which for a large share of the market matters more than correlation depth.

Strengths: By far the most approachable console; guided investigations for teams without hunting experience; synchronized security across endpoint, firewall, and email; clear escalation path into incident response tools and MDR services; the February 2025 Secureworks acquisition adds Counter Threat Unit research depth.

Trade-offs: data coverage and correlation depth trail the leaders; less suited to mature SOCs wanting flexible query and hunting; post-acquisition portfolio positioning is a fair question.

Ideal buyer: mid-market organizations without dedicated security analysts.

Verify before buying: retention limits at your tier, and how Secureworks capability is being positioned.

Image ALT: Sophos XDR guided investigation and cross-product detection

10. eSentire — 7.2/10 eSentire Atlas XDR cross-source threat detection and response platform

Why it scores here: eSentire’s Atlas XDR platform correlates telemetry across endpoint, network, cloud, identity, and other security sources, combining automated detection with 24/7 security operations and threat hunting.

Strengths: open XDR architecture; broad telemetry coverage; strong managed detection and response capabilities; 24/7 threat hunting and human-led investigation can significantly reduce the workload for internal security teams.

Trade-offs: the platform is closely tied to eSentire’s managed security model, so organizations wanting a purely self-operated XDR platform should evaluate the level of control and operational involvement available; pricing is generally quote-based.

Ideal buyer: organizations with heterogeneous security environments that want open XDR capabilities combined with managed detection, threat hunting, and response.

Verify before buying: third-party integrations, telemetry ingestion requirements, response automation capabilities, and the exact level of 24/7 SOC coverage included in your contract.

Image ALT: eSentire Atlas XDR cross-source threat detection and response platform

Head-to-Head Comparisons Buyers Actually Make

Cortex XDR vs CrowdStrike. Cortex correlates a wider native data set, particularly network; CrowdStrike has better endpoint telemetry, threat intelligence, and managed hunting. If you own Palo Alto firewalls, Cortex is the stronger answer.

If endpoint is your centre of gravity and you want human hunters, CrowdStrike is.

Microsoft Defender XDR vs everyone. In an E5 estate, Defender XDR is close to free and genuinely good across Microsoft’s surface.

The question is never whether it’s adequate it usually is but whether concentrating detection with your productivity vendor is acceptable, and what your third-party data costs once you add Sentinel.

XDR vs SIEM. They overlap and increasingly converge. XDR correlates security telemetry into incidents with less engineering effort; SIEM ingests everything including non-security logs and requires you to build detections.

Most mature organizations run both. Small teams should start with XDR, because a SIEM nobody has time to tune produces nothing.

Buyer’s Guide

Audit your telemetry sources before taking quotes. List every source you need correlated endpoints, firewalls, email, identity provider, cloud accounts, SaaS applications and mark which are native to each vendor. That table decides your shortlist faster than any feature comparison.

Model ingestion cost explicitly. XDR pricing is increasingly data-volume-driven, and this is where budgets break. Get a written estimate based on your actual log volume, with a stated overage policy.

Measure alert reduction in the proof of concept. The metric that matters is incidents per week that require analyst attention, compared with what your current tooling produces. If XDR doesn’t reduce that number, it hasn’t done its job.

Decide the native-versus-open question first. It’s architectural and it determines everything downstream, including whether the platform you buy will still fit in three years.

Common mistakes: buying XDR while leaving identity telemetry out of scope, when identity is where most modern attacks progress; assuming XDR replaces the need for managed detection and response when nobody is watching overnight; and paying platform prices to correlate third-party data poorly.

Frequently Asked Questions What is XDR?

Extended detection and response correlates security telemetry from multiple sources endpoints, network, email, identity, and cloud into unified incidents, applying analytics across the combined data rather than treating each source separately.

The goal is fewer, higher-quality incidents instead of more alerts from more consoles.

What is the best XDR platform in 2026?

Palo Alto Cortex XDR scores highest on data coverage and correlation depth, with CrowdStrike close behind on detection engineering and threat intelligence.

Microsoft Defender XDR is the rational choice for Microsoft 365 E5 organizations, and SentinelOne Singularity offers the strongest response automation for small teams.

What is the difference between XDR and SIEM?

XDR correlates security telemetry into incidents with detection content the vendor provides and maintains. SIEM ingests logs from anywhere, including non-security sources, and generally requires you to build and tune your own detections.

XDR is faster to value; SIEM is more flexible and better for compliance log retention. Many organizations run both.

What is open XDR versus native XDR?

Native XDR correlates telemetry the vendor collects with its own products, giving deeper and faster correlation at the cost of vendor consolidation.

Open XDR treats third-party telemetry as a first-class source, letting you keep existing tools with generally shallower correlation. Choose based on how standardized your estate already is.

Do I need XDR if I have EDR?

Not necessarily. If endpoints are your main risk surface and your team is small, good EDR with strong automation may be sufficient. XDR earns its cost when attacks progress across surfaces phishing to endpoint to identity to cloud and you need those events connected.

Most EDR vendors sell XDR as a licensing tier above EDR.

How much do XDR platforms cost?

XDR is typically priced per endpoint or per user, plus data ingestion charges that scale with log volume. Microsoft Defender XDR is included in Microsoft 365 E5.

Everything else is largely quote-based, and ingestion cost is the variable that most often causes budget overruns model it explicitly before signing.

Bottom Line

Palo Alto Cortex XDR takes the top score for correlation depth and native data breadth, and it is the right answer for Palo Alto estates with a SOC.

CrowdStrike is the pick when endpoint detection quality and managed hunting matter most, SentinelOne when automation must substitute for headcount, and Microsoft Defender XDR when you already hold E5 the economics there are hard to argue with.

Sophos deserves serious consideration from mid-market teams precisely because they’ll actually use it.

Settle the native-versus-open question first, then model your ingestion cost. Those two decisions determine whether XDR reduces your workload or just relocates it.

items.title: Top 10 Best Web Application Firewall (WAF) Solutions in 2026
items.summary: A web application firewall (WAF) filters malicious HTTP/S traffic SQL injection, cross-site scripting, credential stuffing, and API abuse before it reaches your applications. Cloudflare is our top WAF pick for 2026 on the strength of protection-per-dollar and a massive attack-visibility network, with Akamai and Imperva holding the enterprise depth tier and AWS WAF owning cloud-native economics. Below, the ten best WAF solutions ranked by security efficacy, deployment fit, and total cost. How a WAF Works A WAF inspects HTTP/S traffic using predefined rules or policies to detect malicious patterns. Here’s how it operates: Traffic Inspection : It examines HTTP methods (e.g., GET, POST), headers, query strings, and request bodies for suspicious activity. Filtering Models : Negative Security Model : Blocks known malicious patterns or signatures. Positive Security Model : Allows only known legitimate traffic while scrutinizing anomalies. Real-Time Blocking : Malicious requests are blocked before reaching the web server, while legitimate traffic is allowed through. Data Protection : Prevents sensitive data leakage by masking or blocking certain responses. Deployment Modes : Commonly deployed as a reverse proxy, ensuring all traffic passes through the WAF for inspection. Quick Verdict • Best overall / best value: Cloudflare — managed rules on a huge network, free to enterprise • Best for highest-traffic enterprise: Akamai — edge scale plus market-leading bot defense • Best detection accuracy: Imperva — the compliance-grade WAF benchmark • Best for AWS-native stacks: AWS WAF — pay-as-you-go, IaC-native • Best for Fortinet estates: Fortinet FortiWeb — ML-based WAF inside the Security Fabric # Solution Best for Standout capability Pricing 1 Cloudflare Value at any scale Managed rules on massive network Free → published → quote 2 Akamai Highest-traffic enterprise Edge scale + bot management Quote (contract) 3 Imperva Compliance-driven enterprise Detection accuracy + WAAP Quote 4 F5 Security-critical apps Advanced WAF + programmability Quote; SaaS tiers 5 AWS WAF AWS-native stacks Usage-priced, IaC-native Pay-as-you-go 6 Fortinet (FortiWeb) Fortinet estates ML anomaly detection License + bundles 7 Barracuda Mid-market simplicity Approachable WAF/WAAP Published + quote 8 Radware DDoS-exposed apps WAF + behavioral DDoS Quote 9 Fastly DevOps velocity teams Low-false-positive Next-Gen WAF Quote (per-app) 10 Microsoft Azure WAF Azure-native apps Native Front Door/App Gateway WAF Usage-based How We Evaluated Research-based ranking, no lab testing claimed. Five criteria: security efficacy (OWASP Top 10 coverage, bot management, API protection, DDoS), deployment fit (CDN-edge, appliance, cloud-native), false-positive discipline and managed-rule quality, ecosystem alignment, and total cost including bot/API modules. Independent context the October 2025 F5 breach (CISA Emergency Directive 26-01)  factored into vendor-risk scoring. Pricing is cited only where published. The 10 Best WAF Solutions in 2026 1. Cloudflare — Best WAF Overall Cloudflare — Best WAF Overall Best for: organizations of any size that want strong protection running in minutes. Cloudflare’s WAF deploys with a DNS change: managed rulesets tuned by visibility into a vast share of global web traffic, a genuinely useful free tier, and published Pro/Business plans bundling CDN, DDoS, and bot mitigation. For most sites below extreme enterprise scale, it’s the best protection-per-effort ratio available. Key features: •             Managed and custom WAF rules updated from massive threat visibility •             Bot management and API Shield (discovery, schema validation) •             DDoS protection and CDN included across tiers •             Rate limiting and page/rule-level controls •             Published pricing from free through Business; enterprise by quote Pros: effortless deployment; transparent pricing; constant rule updates; DDoS+CDN+WAF in one. Cons: deep customization and granular logging push you to enterprise tiers; you adopt Cloudflare as your front door. Pricing: free tier; published Pro/Business; enterprise quote. [VERIFY: current tier prices] Standout differentiator: rule quality maintained by one of the largest attack-visibility footprints on the internet. 2. Akamai — Best for Highest-Traffic Enterprises Akamai — Best for Highest-Traffic Enterprises Best for: enterprises whose applications draw serious traffic and serious adversaries. Akamai’s App & API Protector runs on the platform that pioneered the CDN-edge WAF: adaptive protections tuned by Akamai’s threat research, bot management that leads independent evaluations, API discovery, and DDoS absorption at a scale few networks match. Key features: •             Adaptive, self-tuning WAF protections •             Market-leading bot management •             API discovery and protection •             Edge-scale DDoS absorption •             Premium managed security services Pros: massive edge scale; top-tier bot and API defense; adaptive tuning reduces admin load. Cons: enterprise pricing and contracts; full value needs traffic on Akamai’s platform. Pricing: quote-based enterprise contracts. Standout differentiator: when attack volume and sophistication both spike, Akamai’s capacity is the insurance policy. 3. Imperva — Best Detection Accuracy Imperva — Best Detection Accuracy Best for: regulated enterprises where a missed attack or failed audit costs real money. Imperva has been the WAF accuracy benchmark for over a decade: precise managed rules, a near-zero-tuning reputation, and deployment choices (cloud WAAP, appliance, hybrid) that fit conservative architectures. Under Thales ownership, it anchors a full application-security portfolio with bots, API security, and DDoS. Key features: •             High-accuracy managed rules •             Full WAAP: bot management, API security, DDoS with SLA •             Cloud, appliance, and hybrid deployment •             Advanced threat intelligence (Imperva research) •             Strong audit and compliance tooling Pros: elite detection accuracy reputation; auditors trust it; on-prem option for data residency. Cons: premium pricing; console breadth feels heavyweight for simple needs. Pricing: quote-based. Standout differentiator: signal quality — SOCs trust Imperva verdicts, and managed rules keep protection current without a tuning team. 4. F5 — Best for Security-Critical Applications F5 — Best for Security-Critical Applications Best for: enterprises whose applications justify the deepest available traffic-security stack. F5 spans BIG-IP Advanced WAF (hardware/virtual), NGINX App Protect, and Distributed Cloud WAAP (SaaS). Advanced WAF, per-app policies, iRules programmability, and mature TLS handling remain a reference standard. The honest counterweight: the October 2025 breach of F5’s development environment a nation-state actor exfiltrated BIG-IP source code and vulnerability data triggered CISA Emergency Directive 26-01. F5 has shipped hardened releases; demand its post-incident roadmap and patch-SLA commitments. Key features: •             Advanced WAF with behavioral bot defense •             API discovery and protection •             iRules programmability and full-proxy TLS •             Hardware, virtual, cloud, and SaaS delivery •             Distributed Cloud WAAP for modern stacks Pros: unmatched feature depth and programmability; huge talent pool; flexible consumption. Cons: 2025 breach damaged trust — scrutinize patch SLAs; premium pricing; real expertise required. Pricing: quote-based across perpetual, subscription, SaaS. Standout differentiator: breadth — legacy hardware ADC-WAF through cloud-native API security in one portfolio. 5. AWS WAF — Best for AWS-Native Stacks AWS WAF — Best for AWS-Native Stacks Best for: teams whose applications, load balancers, and APIs already live on AWS. AWS WAF attaches natively to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and AppSync — pay-as-you-go, IaC-friendly, with managed rule groups from AWS and Marketplace vendors. No new vendor, no new network path. Key features: •             Native attachment to AWS services •             Per-rule, per-request published pricing •             Managed rule groups (AWS + Marketplace) •             Infrastructure-as-code support (CloudFormation/Terraform) •             Pairs with AWS Shield for DDoS Pros: native integration; transparent usage pricing; strong IaC support; no minimums. Cons: it’s a toolkit — rule quality is what you configure or buy; single-cloud only. Pricing: published pay-as-you-go (per web ACL, rule, and million requests). Standout differentiator: the integration is the product — protection lands exactly where AWS traffic already flows. 6. Fortinet FortiWeb — Best for Fortinet Estates Fortinet FortiWeb — Best for Fortinet Estates Best for: organizations already running Fortinet who want WAF under familiar management. FortiWeb pairs appliance/VM licensing with ML-based anomaly detection, bot mitigation, and API protection, plus native Security Fabric integration. FortiWeb Cloud (SaaS) covers lighter needs at published entry pricing. Key features: •             Machine-learning anomaly detection (dual-layer ML) •             Bot mitigation and API protection •             Security Fabric integration with FortiGate •             Hardware, VM, and SaaS delivery •             Credential-stuffing and threat-analytics tooling Pros: strong bundle value for Fortinet shops; one-vendor operations; broad form factors. Cons: heavier console than cloud-native rivals; best value inside the Fabric. Pricing: appliance/VM license plus bundles; FortiWeb Cloud published entry tiers. Standout differentiator: ML anomaly detection that adapts to each application’s normal traffic pattern. 7. Barracuda — Best Mid-Market Simplicity Barracuda — Best Mid-Market Simplicity Best for: mid-market organizations wanting capable WAF without enterprise complexity. Barracuda’s WAF (appliance/virtual) and WAF-as-a-Service extend the vendor’s keep-it-simple philosophy to application security: sensible defaults, bundled DDoS and bot protection, and consolidated support with the rest of a Barracuda estate. Key features: •             WAF appliance, virtual, and WAF-as-a-Service •             Bundled DDoS and bot protection •             API security and automated learning •             Vulnerability-scanner integration •             Central management Pros: approachable administration; WAFaaS for quick starts; fair mid-market pricing. Cons: less independent test visibility than leaders; advanced API depth trails Imperva/Akamai. Pricing: published ranges via resellers plus quotes. Standout differentiator: the simplicity a lean IT team can actually run in blocking mode. 8. Radware — Best for DDoS-Exposed Applications Radware — Best for DDoS-Exposed Applications Best for: finance, gaming, and e-commerce platforms where web attacks and DDoS arrive together. Radware’s WAF (AppWall/Cloud WAF) integrates the company’s specialty behavioral DDoS mitigation with a well-regarded WAF, SSL inspection, and bot management in one chassis or cloud service. Key features: •             Behavioral-based DDoS protection •             ICSA-certified WAF heritage •             Bot manager and API protection •             SSL offload/inspection •             Global elastic licensing across hybrid estates Pros: attack-mitigation depth most WAF vendors lack; strong analytics; flexible licensing. Cons: smaller market share and community; management UX trails cloud-first rivals. Pricing: quote-based. Standout differentiator: a WAF built by a DDoS-mitigation company availability and application security in one. 9. Fastly — Best for DevOps-Velocity Teams Fastly — Best for DevOps-Velocity Teams Best for: engineering organizations shipping daily who refuse to babysit false positives. Fastly’s Next-Gen WAF (Signal Sciences lineage) keeps its developer-loved DNA: install at the edge, as an agent/module, or in Kubernetes; get meaningful decisions via SmartParse rather than regex noise; wire alerts into Slack, PagerDuty, and CI/CD. Key features: •             SmartParse detection with low false positives •             Flexible deployment (edge, agent, Kubernetes) •             Strong API protection •             DevOps-native integrations •             Runs in blocking mode without a tuning priesthood Pros: exceptional signal-to-noise; flexible deployment; engineering-culture fit. Cons: premium per-app pricing; deepest value assumes engineering engagement. Pricing: quote-based, per-app. Standout differentiator: accuracy that lets teams actually block, not just monitor. 10. Microsoft Azure WAF — Best for Azure-Native Apps Microsoft Azure WAF — Best for Azure-Native Apps Best for: organizations delivering applications through Azure Front Door or Application Gateway. Azure WAF is the native, managed option: policies attach to Front Door (global) or Application Gateway (regional), with Microsoft-managed and custom rule sets, bot protection, and Sentinel integration usage-priced and simple for Azure-first estates. Key features: •             Native Front Door and Application Gateway integration •             Microsoft-managed and custom rule sets (OWASP CRS) •             Bot protection rules •             Sentinel/Monitor logging integration •             Usage-based pricing Pros: native Azure integration and billing simplicity; managed rule sets; Sentinel tie-in. Cons: Azure-only; rule ergonomics and API depth trail dedicated WAAP leaders. Pricing: published usage-based (policy + request volume). [VERIFY: current rates] Standout differentiator: the path of least resistance for protecting Azure-delivered apps. Full Comparison Table Solution Deployment Bot management API security DDoS included Free tier/trial Cloudflare Edge/CDN Yes Yes (API Shield) Yes Free tier Akamai Edge/CDN Best-in-class Yes Yes Trial via sales Imperva SaaS, appliance Yes Yes Yes (SLA) Trial F5 HW, VE, SaaS Yes Yes Add-on XC trial AWS WAF AWS services Via rules Partial Via Shield Pay-per-use FortiWeb HW, VM, SaaS Yes Yes Partner/Fabric Eval Barracuda HW, VM, SaaS Yes Yes Bundled 30-day (typical) Radware Cloud, appliance Yes Yes Core strength Trial Fastly Edge, agent, K8s Yes Yes Via Fastly Trial Azure WAF Azure-native Yes Partial Azure DDoS add-on Pay-per-use How to Choose a WAF in 2026 Start with where traffic should be inspected: a CDN edge (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly edge), inside your cloud (AWS WAF, Azure WAF), or on appliances you control (Imperva, FortiWeb, F5). Weight false-positive economics an accurate WAF saves analyst hours that dwarf license deltas, so teams without security engineers should favor managed-rule quality (Imperva, Cloudflare, Fastly). API-heavy businesses must demand API discovery and schema enforcement, not just OWASP coverage. After 2025’s F5 breach, put vendor patch velocity and breach transparency into the RFP. And whatever you deploy, run it in blocking mode with a rollback plan a monitor-only WAF is a dashboard, not a defense. Pair the WAF with upstream network security and DDoS protection for layered coverage. FAQ What is a web application firewall (WAF)? A WAF inspects HTTP/S traffic at the application layer and blocks attacks like SQL injection, cross-site scripting, credential stuffing, and API abuse before they reach your applications. It complements never replaces network firewalls, which don’t understand application requests. Which WAF is best in 2026? Cloudflare is the best overall for value and ease, Akamai and Imperva lead enterprise depth (scale/bot defense and detection accuracy respectively), and AWS WAF or Azure WAF win for single-cloud native stacks. Fastly is the pick for engineering teams that demand low false positives. What is WAAP, and how is it different from WAF? WAAP (web application and API protection) is the expanded category: classic WAF plus bot management, API security, and DDoS mitigation in one platform. Most leaders here Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva, F5, Fastly sell WAAP even when buyers still say “WAF.” Should I worry about the F5 breach if I use BIG-IP? Take it seriously, not fatally. A nation-state actor stole BIG-IP source code and vulnerability data (disclosed October 2025), and CISA Emergency Directive 26-01 ordered rapid patching. Run the latest versions, restrict management-plane exposure, and follow F5’s post-incident guidance. How much does a WAF cost? From free (Cloudflare’s tier) through published SMB pricing to enterprise WAAP contracts in five-to-six figures annually. AWS WAF and Azure WAF publish usage pricing. Bot management and API security modules typically add 30–100% to enterprise quotes — itemize them. Can a WAF protect APIs? Modern WAAPs can, with caveats. A web application firewall (WAF) filters malicious HTTP/S traffic SQL injection, cross-site scripting, credential stuffing, and API abuse before it reaches your applications.

Cloudflare is our top WAF pick for 2026 on the strength of protection-per-dollar and a massive attack-visibility network, with Akamai and Imperva holding the enterprise depth tier and AWS WAF owning cloud-native economics.

Below, the ten best WAF solutions ranked by security efficacy, deployment fit, and total cost.

How a WAF Works

A WAF inspects HTTP/S traffic using predefined rules or policies to detect malicious patterns. Here’s how it operates:

  • Traffic Inspection: It examines HTTP methods (e.g., GET, POST), headers, query strings, and request bodies for suspicious activity.
  • Filtering Models:
  • Negative Security Model: Blocks known malicious patterns or signatures.
  • Positive Security Model: Allows only known legitimate traffic while scrutinizing anomalies.
  • Real-Time Blocking: Malicious requests are blocked before reaching the web server, while legitimate traffic is allowed through.
  • Data Protection: Prevents sensitive data leakage by masking or blocking certain responses.
  • Deployment Modes: Commonly deployed as a reverse proxy, ensuring all traffic passes through the WAF for inspection.
Quick Verdict

•             Best overall / best value: Cloudflare — managed rules on a huge network, free to enterprise

•             Best for highest-traffic enterprise: Akamai — edge scale plus market-leading bot defense

•             Best detection accuracy: Imperva — the compliance-grade WAF benchmark

•             Best for AWS-native stacks: AWS WAF — pay-as-you-go, IaC-native

•             Best for Fortinet estates: Fortinet FortiWeb — ML-based WAF inside the Security Fabric

Start with where traffic should be inspected: a CDN edge (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly edge), inside your cloud (AWS WAF, Azure WAF), or on appliances you control (Imperva, FortiWeb, F5).

Weight false-positive economics an accurate WAF saves analyst hours that dwarf license deltas, so teams without security engineers should favor managed-rule quality (Imperva, Cloudflare, Fastly).

API-heavy businesses must demand API discovery and schema enforcement, not just OWASP coverage. After 2025’s F5 breach, put vendor patch velocity and breach transparency into the RFP.

And whatever you deploy, run it in blocking mode with a rollback plan a monitor-only WAF is a dashboard, not a defense. Pair the WAF with upstream network security and DDoS protection for layered coverage.

FAQ What is a web application firewall (WAF)?

A WAF inspects HTTP/S traffic at the application layer and blocks attacks like SQL injection, cross-site scripting, credential stuffing, and API abuse before they reach your applications.

It complements never replaces network firewalls, which don’t understand application requests.

Which WAF is best in 2026?

Cloudflare is the best overall for value and ease, Akamai and Imperva lead enterprise depth (scale/bot defense and detection accuracy respectively), and AWS WAF or Azure WAF win for single-cloud native stacks.

Fastly is the pick for engineering teams that demand low false positives.

What is WAAP, and how is it different from WAF?

WAAP (web application and API protection) is the expanded category: classic WAF plus bot management, API security, and DDoS mitigation in one platform.

Most leaders here Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva, F5, Fastly sell WAAP even when buyers still say “WAF.”

Should I worry about the F5 breach if I use BIG-IP?

Take it seriously, not fatally. A nation-state actor stole BIG-IP source code and vulnerability data (disclosed October 2025), and CISA Emergency Directive 26-01 ordered rapid patching.

Run the latest versions, restrict management-plane exposure, and follow F5’s post-incident guidance.

How much does a WAF cost?

From free (Cloudflare’s tier) through published SMB pricing to enterprise WAAP contracts in five-to-six figures annually. AWS WAF and Azure WAF publish usage pricing.

Bot management and API security modules typically add 30–100% to enterprise quotes — itemize them.

Can a WAF protect APIs?

Modern WAAPs can, with caveats. Look for API discovery (finding endpoints you forgot), schema validation, and abuse detection not just signature rules.

Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva, F5, and Fastly lead here; verify API depth explicitly if APIs carry your revenue.

Conclusion

Cloudflare leads 2026’s WAF field on value and reach, Akamai and Imperva on enterprise depth, and AWS/Azure WAF on cloud-native economics with FortiWeb, Barracuda, Radware, and Fastly winning their ecosystem, mid-market, DDoS-coupled, and DevOps niches.

items.title: CYBER HUNTER PROJECT Book — What You Will Find Inside
items.summary: Here it is! :) One of my main goals for 2026 has arrived a little later than expected, but it is finally here: the CYBER HUNTER PROJECT book. I have to say that writing a book from scratch has been quite an adventure. I have learned a lot about all the challenges and difficulties involved in taking an idea and turning it into a published book. I hope you enjoy it — and if you decide to grab a copy, you will be helping me turn all that effort into a well-earned beer or coffee! 🍺☕ Why I Wrote This Book Over the years, I have created many hunts to investigate real situations. Some started with an alert, others with a suspicion, and quite a few with a simple thought: what if this is happening in my environment and nobody is looking for it? Many of those hunts later became articles, public projects, and queries. This book is where I bring that work together and explain what led me to each investigation. This is not a book built by following an existing framework or repeating ideas from other books. It comes from personal experience: investigations I have worked on, queries I have written, things that did not work as expected, and lessons I learned by doing the job. I do not want you to copy a query, run it, and stop there. I want you to understand why the hunt started, what evidence to look for, and how to turn the result into something useful. If this book makes you more curious about your own environment and encourages you to start looking before an alert tells you something is wrong, then it has done its job. That became CYBER HUNTER PROJECT. The idea was to create the kind of Threat Hunting reference I would like to have next to me while working: practical, easy to navigate and focused on investigations rather than hundreds of pages of theory. The book contains 32 practical Threat Hunting investigations across Email, Endpoints, Networks, Threat Intelligence, Identity, Software and Cloud Applications. The scenarios are very different. You will find hunts around Phishing, unusual email activity, suspicious process execution, DNS behaviour, network connections, authentication anomalies, software running across the environment, Threat Intelligence and activity inside Cloud Applications. But the important part for me was not simply providing a query for each case. What you will find inside When I started putting CYBER HUNTER PROJECT together, one thing was clear to me: I did not want to create a book full of theory and then add a few queries at the end. I wanted to build something practical. Something close to what we actually do when we sit in front of the telemetry and start asking questions. That is why the main part of the book is built around 32 Threat Hunting investigations across Email, Endpoints, Networks, Threat Intelligence, Identity, Software and Cloud Applications. You will find hunts around Phishing and malicious URLs, suspicious processes and LOLBins, DNS and unusual network activity, identity and authentication behaviour, Threat Intelligence pivots, software running in the environment, Cloud Applications and many other scenarios. But before running a query, we need a reason to run it. So I also spend time on Hunt Hypotheses, IOC vs IOA, baselines, risk scoring and how we move from a simple “something here looks strange” to telemetry, evidence and finally a hunt. Something else I wanted to include is what happens after we find something. Can this behaviour become a detection? Can we stop what is happening? Did it actually have an impact? Can we respond? This is where the Detection Opportunities and the HUNTER Decision Cycle come into the book. The methodology throughout the book is vendor-neutral, while the companion queries are written in KQL, simply because this is the technology I work with every day. The idea is not to copy/paste them and call it done. Take the logic, test it, change it and adapt it to your own environment. So inside the book you will find investigations, queries, diagrams, Detection Opportunities and, especially, ideas that hopefully give you another place to start your next hunt. That was the goal when I started putting all of this together. Beyond the investigations So that is what you will find inside CYBER HUNTER PROJECT: real hunting scenarios, the thinking behind them, evidence analysis and Detection Opportunities that you can adapt to your own environment. A book designed to be read, but also to stay next to your computer when you need an idea for your next hunt. 📔 CYBER HUNTER PROJECT is now available on Amazon. items.title: Hackers Hijack Coder Registry to Push Malicious Terraform Modules and Steal Cloud Credentials
items.summary: A critical security incident at Coder exposed users of its Terraform module registry to malicious packages designed to steal credentials from cloud development environments. The attack involved unauthorized changes to Coder’s Cloudflare infrastructure, allowing an unidentified threat actor to redirect some registry traffic to attacker-controlled servers. According to Coder’s security advisory, the attacker added unauthorized IP addresses to the infrastructure pool used by the Coder module registry. Those servers hosted a rogue registry containing modified Terraform artifacts with credential-stealing code. The affected service was Coder’s main registry, registry.coder.com, which is commonly used as a source of workspace templates and modules. The malicious packages were available between 07:35 UTC and 21:45 UTC on August 31, 2026. Organizations may have been exposed if they created a new Coder workspace template, updated an existing template version, ran a template dry run, or deployed a workspace. At the same time, Terraform module caching was disabled. Hackers Hijack Coder Registry The injected code targeted secrets available to the Terraform provisioner environment. Coder said the malware attempted to identify credentials and exfiltrate them to a remote server using a lookalike domain, coder-infra[.]com. The domain was designed to resemble legitimate Coder infrastructure, making malicious outbound connections harder to identify during routine log reviews. The malicious Terraform modules reportedly used a data.external.telemetry block to execute a script named dlp-docker.sh. That script communicated with the attacker-controlled endpoint at www[.]coder-infra[.]com/cli/check and sent data through an X-CLI-Token HTTP header. The advisory identified 199.91.220[.]205 as an associated IP address. The impact depends on how the malicious module was executed. During template imports, updates, and dry runs, the primary risk was exposure of environment variables and secrets available on the provisioner host. In a workspace build, the malicious code could also access temporary user secrets passed to the provisioner. These may include a user OIDC token, an SSH key where configured, and one-time external authentication tokens. Organizations running the provisioner within the main Coder service may face a broader exposure. In that deployment model, the malware may have accessed Coder configuration values, including database credentials, external authentication provider settings, and other application secrets. Coder stated in its GitHub advisory GHSA-vx42-ghc9-gw65 that there was no indication that customer data maintained by the company was affected. Coder released patched versions 2.37.0, 2.36.4, 2.35.7, and 2.34.9. Users running versions earlier than 2.37.0 should remove potentially malicious registry modules from their cache and update. Security teams should review Coder deployment records for module downloads within the affected window and search DNS, firewall, proxy, and VPC flow logs for connections to coder-infra[.]com. They should also inspect provisioner logs for the string data.external.telemetry, which can indicate execution of the malicious Terraform block. Affected organizations should remove cached modules retrieved during the exposure period before redeploying templates. They should then rotate all credentials that could have been accessible to the Coder deployment, particularly cloud API keys, CI/CD secrets , AI tooling tokens, SSH keys, OIDC tokens, and credentials stored in environment variables or terminal history. The incident highlights a supply-chain risk in infrastructure-as-code workflows. Even trusted Terraform registries can become a route for credential theft when attackers compromise traffic-routing or package-distribution infrastructure. The injected code targeted secrets available to the Terraform provisioner environment. Coder said the malware attempted to identify credentials and exfiltrate them to a remote server using a lookalike domain, coder-infra[.]com.

The domain was designed to resemble legitimate Coder infrastructure, making malicious outbound connections harder to identify during routine log reviews. The malicious Terraform modules reportedly used a data.external.telemetry block to execute a script named dlp-docker.sh.

That script communicated with the attacker-controlled endpoint at www[.]coder-infra[.]com/cli/check and sent data through an X-CLI-Token HTTP header. The advisory identified 199.91.220[.]205 as an associated IP address.

The impact depends on how the malicious module was executed. During template imports, updates, and dry runs, the primary risk was exposure of environment variables and secrets available on the provisioner host.

In a workspace build, the malicious code could also access temporary user secrets passed to the provisioner. These may include a user OIDC token, an SSH key where configured, and one-time external authentication tokens.

Organizations running the provisioner within the main Coder service may face a broader exposure. In that deployment model, the malware may have accessed Coder configuration values, including database credentials, external authentication provider settings, and other application secrets.

Coder stated in its GitHub advisory GHSA-vx42-ghc9-gw65 that there was no indication that customer data maintained by the company was affected.

Coder released patched versions 2.37.0, 2.36.4, 2.35.7, and 2.34.9. Users running versions earlier than 2.37.0 should remove potentially malicious registry modules from their cache and update.

Security teams should review Coder deployment records for module downloads within the affected window and search DNS, firewall, proxy, and VPC flow logs for connections to coder-infra[.]com.

They should also inspect provisioner logs for the string data.external.telemetry, which can indicate execution of the malicious Terraform block. Affected organizations should remove cached modules retrieved during the exposure period before redeploying templates.

They should then rotate all credentials that could have been accessible to the Coder deployment, particularly cloud API keys, CI/CD secrets, AI tooling tokens, SSH keys, OIDC tokens, and credentials stored in environment variables or terminal history.

The incident highlights a supply-chain risk in infrastructure-as-code workflows. Even trusted Terraform registries can become a route for credential theft when attackers compromise traffic-routing or package-distribution infrastructure.

items.title: Testing race conditions with memory access tracing and stack-based delay injection
items.summary:
Many security bugs are race conditions, where multi-threaded execution has to occur with the right interleaving for a negative effect to appear. This creates challenges for several use cases: Confirming bug candidates that have been discovered manually or through static analysis. Regression tests: After fixing a race condition bug, there is often no good way to write a regression test that reliably triggers the bug as part of a test suite. Automatic bug discovery, such as fuzzing: It is hard for a fuzzer to exercise all interesting interleavings of concurrent operations, or reach code paths that are only exercised when operations are racing. I mostly discover bugs by manually reading code. When I think I’ve found a bug, I normally write a test case to either prove or disprove that the bug exists. For race condition bugs, it can be hard to achieve either outcome. For Linux kernel bugs, I often resort to recompiling the kernel after adding conditional mdelay() calls (which spinloop for roughly the specified amount of time) in appropriate places; I usually make these conditional based on the name of the running thread, though sometimes more complex conditions are needed. On platforms that support DTrace (like macOS and Windows ), it is possible to use DTrace probes that call chill() for similar effect, though the utility of this is limited as DTrace can only trace on non-inline function boundaries or explicit trace points, rather than on every instruction. Regardless of platform, this approach can be time consuming and can require trial and error to definitely determine whether code is buggy. Additionally, in the Linux kernel, fixes for race condition bugs are often accompanied by hand-written ASCII diagrams showing problematic thread interleavings with call graphs and relevant memory accesses (for example, see this recent rt_spin_unlock UAF fix , or this recent jbd2 deadlock fix ). It would be convenient to have developer tooling that can analyze potentially vulnerable code and show results in a similar representation. Summary I wrote tools for exploring possible interleavings of multi-threaded test cases for the Linux kernel: A tool that automatically tests all possible A-B-A interleavings of a test case. A terminal UI for manual exploration of possible interleavings. A GUI for manual exploration of possible interleavings. The kernel part of this is intended to also be usable for discovering race conditions via fuzzing, but userspace tooling for that still needs to be implemented. The tools are available on GitHub under the name MAccConc, short for “Memory Access Concurrency”; see the README there for installation and usage instructions. If you just want to see the tooling in action, skip to Demo: automatic testing . If you’re just interested in the theory behind the tooling, read section Stable identifiers for memory accesses across runs: count-augmented stack traces . Prior work This project was inspired by discussions with Ned Williamson, whose sockfuzzer project involved exploration of concurrency bugs by using a custom scheduler that can reschedule at synchronization primitives to explore interleavings. See the conference talk slides and recording focused on the concurrency testing aspect of this. My tooling is largely based on ideas similar to SKI , but SKI uses a different implementation: It records memory accesses and controls scheduling of vCPUs using a patched version of QEMU in TCG mode, and uses VM snapshots to explore different execution interleavings. Discovering memory accesses that could contribute to race conditions (communication points) As described in the SKI paper, interesting execution interleavings of a given multi-threaded test case can be discovered by tracing memory accesses of all threads and searching for pairs of accesses on two threads that could interact with each other - meaning, roughly, that at least one of them is a write operation, and they access overlapping memory ranges. The SKI paper calls such memory accesses communication points . This requires some mechanism to collect memory access coverage. SKI did this by patching QEMU’s TCG mode; I am instead relying on ASAN instrumentation in “outline” mode (compiler backend flag asan-instrumentation-with-call-threshold=0 , selected by CONFIG_KASAN_OUTLINE in the Linux kernel), which generates helper function calls on memory access. I believe that the kernel is the right place to collect this data because it would allow the kernel to also provide higher-level information about lock acquire/release events and such, though I have not implemented this at this time. Implementing this in the kernel also means that it would theoretically be possible to test on bare-metal hardware, rather than inside VMs. Since Linux already has KCOV as a mechanism to feed basic block kernel coverage information to userspace, I decided to use the same mechanism to record information about memory accesses. An alternative would have been to use ftrace, which is oriented towards tracing use cases, and includes a function graph tracing mode built on fentry hooks and more complex output buffer management that is oriented towards use cases including system-wide data collection. I chose to use KCOV because of its simpler in-memory representation of trace data (which could become relevant for recovering trace data from crashed VMs); because it uses static always-on instrumentation rather than runtime-enabled instrumentation with near-zero overhead in disabled state; and because my impression is that KCOV is designed for higher-frequency trace events than ftrace. Implementation detail: ASAN and TSAN ASAN normally merges helper calls for subsequent memory accesses. To receive one callback per memory access, the kernel patches explicitly disable this compiler optimization using the asan-opt-same-temp backend flag. ASAN is intended for identifying UAF, so it does not emit helper calls on direct stack memory access unless there is potential for out-of-bounds access. This means that some race conditions involving on-stack objects, such as wait queues, may not be detectable with this. ASAN also by default emits no helper calls for access to globals, but this optimization can be disabled using the asan-opt-globals backend flag. An alternative would be to use TSAN instrumentation instead, which is designed for detecting data races and also provides information about access atomicity. The downside of TSAN instrumentation is that compilers do not support emitting both ASAN and TSAN hooks at the same time - so to still have working detection of memory safety violations (like UAF) while using TSAN hooks, it would be necessary to run the kernel’s ASAN implementation off of the TSAN hooks or change the compiler. Implementation detail: KCOV and background work Some race conditions involve background work, for example: receive processing of loopback network packets RCU callbacks KCOV can optionally collect remote coverage for background work in some subsystems; however, in upstream Linux, most types of background work that would be interesting for me are not yet integrated with this mechanism, and remote coverage is currently mainly used for fuzzing subsystems that handle incoming data from devices, like bluetooth and USB. Enabling this for other parts of the kernel should be relatively straightforward, and I have a draft patch for doing this for RCU callbacks. Stable identifiers for memory accesses across runs: count-augmented stack traces To test out different orderings of memory accesses, a way to stably identify interesting memory accesses across test case executions is needed. Identifying memory accesses based on the data address would not work if the data address was located in an object which is freshly allocated during each test case execution; and identifying memory accesses solely by instruction address would not work well if the memory access was in a function like memcpy() or spin_lock() . SKI solves this using VM state snapshots, so that each execution starts from the same global state. I am instead identifying memory accesses with count-augmented stack traces, where each stack trace element essentially consists of a callee function address and a number indicating how many calls to this callee should be skipped in the calling stack frame. An example of the semantics of a count-augmented stack trace would be something like: “On this thread, look at the second call to __x64_sys_recvfrom , then within that, the first call to __sys_recvfrom , then within that the first call to sock_recvmsg , then within that, the first call to unix_stream_recvmsg , then within that, the first call to unix_stream_read_generic , then within that, the second call to _raw_spin_unlock , and then within that, the first memory access at instruction address X”. This unambiguously identifies a point in an execution trace, is independent of concrete data addresses, and is relatively stable with regards to changes in the control flow of irrelevant parts of the trace. To make this work, KCOV must provide information about function entry/exit events so that when userspace is parsing KCOV coverage output, it can keep track of how the call stack changes. Doing this nicely requires compiler support as part of SanitizerCoverage; I landed an LLVM feature patch for this a few months ago (see documentation ), which landed in the LLVM 23.1.0 release. Forcing execution orderings with delay injection To force specific execution orderings through KCOV, I implemented an ioctl KCOV_SET_DI using which userspace can request that actions (essentially wait/wake) are taken on memory accesses at specific count-augmented stack traces. (See documentation in my kernel branch .) Each action either sets one flag, or waits for one flag to be set, at a userspace-provided index in a shared array of flags. The possible action types are: DI_STACK_WAKE_PRE : before the memory access, set flag N DI_STACK_WAIT : before the memory access, spin-wait until flag N is set DI_STACK_WAKE_POST : after the memory access, set flag N With the same ioctl, userspace also configures an upper limit on spin-wait iterations. Additionally, there are ioctls for userspace to directly interact with the same flags. This API enables two different ways of using delay injection: constraint-style delay injection and fully-specified ordering. Constraint-style delay injection (A-happens-before-B) Userspace can set up a series of A-happens-before-B constraints, where each such constraint is implemented as a pair of actions in different threads that operate on the same flag: DI_STACK_WAKE_POST for the access that should happen first DI_STACK_WAIT for the access that should happen second With this approach, the execution ordering is left partly non-deterministic. This is what the GUI and terminal UI tools currently implement. An advantage is that this is somewhat more intuitive for simple cases; however, it requires recording timing information to show the user approximately in what order events happened, and it can make the execution trace more complicated. It also often requires more constraints than a fully specified ordering, and is more complicated to reason about. Fully specified ordering (context-switch-style) Userspace can decide on a specific ordering in which events should occur, by picking points at which execution should transfer from one context to another. For the simple case with two execution contexts, this requires that thread A starts running a syscall while thread B begins by spin-waiting on a flag; then when thread A reaches some count-augmented stack trace, thread A uses a combination of DI_STACK_WAKE_PRE and DI_STACK_WAIT to pause its own execution and let thread B continue; and later, thread B can do the same to switch back. This is the approach I used for the automatic A-B-A interleaving tester. Demo: automatic testing I’ll explain more background below; but first, here are two shiny demos on a toy example! This is an example of using the automatic A-B-A interleaving tester on this test case with concurrent dup(5) and close(5) calls: #define _GNU_SOURCE
#include #include #include #include #include #include static int test_fd ; static int dup_res , dup_errno ; void test_setup ( void ) { test_fd = open ( "/" , O_PATH ); } void test_thread1 ( void ) { dup_res = dup ( test_fd ); dup_errno = errno ; } void test_thread2 ( void ) { close ( test_fd ); } void test_end ( void ) { printf ( "dup(%d) = %d (%s) \n " , test_fd , dup_res , dup_res == - 1 ? strerror ( dup_errno ) : "success" ); } It discovers one ordering where dup(5) returns 5 , which is working as intended but might be a somewhat surprising result: sh-5.3# ./kcov-autorace testcase/demo-dup-vs-close.so
loading kallsyms
RCU state (excluded): base=ffffffff82970100 len=500
loading testcase
initializing kcov
collecting A-B coverage
dup(5) = 6 (success)
testing candidates
dup(5) = -1 (Bad file descriptor)
dup(5) = -1 (Bad file descriptor)
dup(5) = -1 (Bad file descriptor)
dup(5) = 5 (success)
dup(5) = 6 (success)
dup(5) = 6 (success)
dup(5) = 6 (success)
dup(5) = 6 (success)
dup(5) = 6 (success)
dup(5) = 6 (success)
dup(5) = 6 (success)
stats:  injection-failed:0  wait-timeout:7  reordered:4
sh-5.3# Demo: GUI And here is an example of me using the GUI on the same test case, using it to manually force an ordering where dup(7) returns 7 . First, I launch the GUI, then run the test case once in the guest: sh-5.3# ./kcov-vsock-client testcase/demo-dup-vs-close.so
dup(7) = 8 (success) At this point, no ordering constraints are enforced yet; dup() and close() are racing randomly. The GUI shows in what order execution happened: This current view just shows function call graphs from both threads (thread 1 with black indent, thread 2 with red indent). The close() syscall happened to execute after dup() this time. Normal functions are shown in black; inline functions are shown in green, but only shown if they called a normal function (since “all inline functions” is not ticked). Ticking “filter to communication points” shows a bunch of memory accesses in blue, which are communication points (as defined above, in short: reads from locations to which other threads write and writes to locations which other threads access; kfree() counts as a write operation). Each memory access line shows the type of access (Read/Write/Free), data address, access size, and the memory value before the access. Hovering over an access highlights all overlapping accesses in yellow. Left-clicking on a memory access shows a view that is instead filtered to only show memory accesses overlapping the selected access. Note that this can show reads that were not identified as communication points (because all writes happen on the same thread). Left-clicking a function name shows a source code view on the right, interspersed with trace data. Data values loaded by memory reads are shown in red (under the source line and column to which the compiler attributes the access); data writes are marked similarly with a red “WRITE”; memory accesses that are communication points are prefixed with “INTERFERENCE” in orange. Function calls are shown in blue. By right-clicking on two memory accesses in the call graph view, it is possible to create an ordering constraint between the two accesses, such that the kernel will attempt to make the first selected access happen before the second selected access. Each ordering constraint is shown on the right side, represented as two count-augmented stack traces. Note that the last bottom element of the stack actually identifies a specific instruction, but the UI doesn’t really show this. Also, the count-augmented stack traces shown here do not include inline functions. In this case, I have created one ordering constraint that orders the second file descriptor table access in __fget_files_rcu() (which is inlined into __fget_files() ) before the file descriptor table entry removal in file_close_fd_locked() (which is inlined into file_close_fd() ). This ensures that the file descriptor table lookup in dup() successfully looks up the file descriptor table entry before it is cleared by the concurrent close() . I have created another ordering constraint that orders the spin_unlock(&files->file_lock) in file_close_fd() before the spin_lock(&files->file_lock) in alloc_fd() so that the file descriptor table entry has been released by the time dup() searches for an unused entry. In this view, ordering constraints have been specified, but the test case has not yet been run with this specified ordering. (This view is filtered to show accesses to the files_struct::file_lock.) Now, re-running the test case shows: sh-5.3# ./kcov-vsock-client testcase/demo-dup-vs-close.so
dup(7) = 7 (success) And the new trace appears in the UI, with brown “DELAY INJECTION” lines interspersed to show how the ordering constraints were applied. Note that the UI shows the ordering of events based on timing information that is associated only with memory accesses; the placement for any event other than a memory access is inferred based on that. In views filtered by data accesses, function entry events are additionally only shown at the time of the first displayed non-function-entry event. For example, in the following screenshot, the first thread may have already entered get_unused_fd_flags() by the time file_close_fd() called spin_unlock() , even though the events are shown the other way around. However, memory accesses should be shown in approximately the right order; with the caveats that the order of memory accesses might be wrong if events happened at the same clock value, and that timing information is recorded by instrumentation that runs directly before the actual access. (Building the tool on fully specified orderings instead would avoid such caveats.) (This view is filtered to show accesses to the file descriptor table entry.) More documentation is available inside the GUI. Implementation status For LLVM: The required patch has landed in LLVM 23.1.0. For the Linux kernel: The required patches are not yet in the upstream kernel. I am posting the Linux kernel patch series for upstream review around the same time as this blog post; a git branch with my patches is also available on github (with a few more patches that aren’t yet ready for upstreaming). If you want to test this tooling, you will need to use my kernel branch for now. (See the README in the tools repository for build instructions.) My kernel patches are in a clean state; the userspace tooling is a bit more hacky, in particular the GUI implementation. The command-line tooling can only handle two concurrent threads, while the GUI can handle additional execution contexts (with the kcov-vsock-client harness: background work launched by thread A). I am looking forward to hearing if this is useful to others, and maybe even what tools others manage to build on top of this! Feel free to reach out to me (for example via email to maccconc-tooling@google.com). Future work Use fully specified orderings instead of constraint-style for manual tooling The non-automatic tooling currently uses constraint-style delay injection; but as described above, fully-specified orderings have several advantages, including more deterministic behavior. I might change the GUI implementation to use fully-specified orderings instead in the future. Type information for human-readable memory access traces For reading memory access traces as a human, it might be helpful to provide information on the object types that are being accessed. One way to do this would be to follow what Microsoft’s debugging tools can do with CodeView debuginfo and use debuginfo to associate memory allocation function call sites with type information, then let the allocator track the call sites from which objects have been allocated. I proposed to add such a feature to the DWARF standard , which has been accepted and is included in the current DWARF 6 draft (search for DW_AT_alloc_type ), and added enough support to LLVM to make it work in the same cases where it already worked with CodeView; but so far that only works for C++ new calls, I did not land the changes necessary to make it work for malloc . Making this work in the kernel would require infrastructure that either queries allocator metadata for every memory access record or provides an initial snapshot of heap allocator metadata across the system plus metadata about subsequent memory allocations. Higher-level memory access feedback One inefficiency in my current prototype is that userspace receives no information about the semantics of locking operations. If two threads each perform lots of memory accesses on an object while holding a lock protecting the object, this will generate a large number of potential communication points, but actually a locked section just represents one big communication point. It might be helpful if the kernel provided “lock acquired” and “lock about to be released” events. But that might not be a very general approach, since impossible orderings caused by locking are not so different from impossible orderings caused by things like an object being initialized before it is published to a global pointer or such. Detecting impossible orderings faster: Deadlock detection In my current implementation, when an attempt is made to force an impossible ordering via delay injection, the result is that one thread spins/waits on a lock until another thread reaches the delay injection timeout, which is inefficient. It might help to have integration with lock debugging infrastructure that can detect such a semi-deadlock in simple cases and abort the test case faster. Fuzzing: Building up test cases with potential communication points like Snowboard Snowboard (a project that searches for concurrency bugs caused by interaction between fuzzer-generated single-threaded test cases) used recorded information about memory accesses in single-threaded test cases to identify which test cases could have interesting communication points when executed in parallel. It would be interesting to build something similar on top of this KCOV-based instrumentation. It might also be interesting to use this for single-threaded test case creation: Start by collecting memory access coverage for individual system calls, then use that to determine which syscalls might interact with each other in interesting ways when executed in sequence, and build up longer system call sequences this way. This would be easier using VM snapshots (like SKI), since my approach does not lead to stable data addresses across test case executions; but it would probably be possible by identifying memory locations that are different between test cases abstractly based on allocation sites, as long as allocation site information is available for all objects that are allocated per test case execution. KCOV output to host-shared memory My current tooling loses KCOV output if the kernel under test panics, so it can’t be used for displaying what happened when a kernel crash occurred. For use cases where the kernel under test is a KVM guest, it might be useful to give the host direct access to the KCOV output buffer. One way to do this might be to use pages in a file on virtiofs with DAX as the KCOV output buffer, and allow writing KCOV output into userspace-provided pages.
